title: Report a load run so the timeouts show

blocks.text: Before a peak season the team runs a load test every night: twenty threads call `mux.request` against the test host, and each call adds a `Sample` with how long the thread waited and whether an answer came back. Last season the nightly report said the 99th percentile was under 5 ms, and on the first busy Saturday the help desk took calls from cashiers whose terminals had shown "outcome unknown" after the full timeout. The logs showed the same thing had happened every night in the load test.

The report is built by `LoadReport` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/LoadReport.java`. Finish the three methods marked `TODO`: `nulls`, `latencies` and `percentile`. `percentile` uses the nearest-rank definition its comment gives: with 20 waits, the 95th percentile is the 19th smallest. When you're done, a run whose purchases end in `null` can't produce a report that looks healthy. About ten lines in total.

cases.says: a run where every request is answered gets its count, no nulls, the slowest wait as max and ordered percentiles
the requests that came back null are counted
a request with no answer is a wait as long as the timeout, so it stays in the latencies and shows in the p99
samples arrive in the order requests finish, so the waits must be ordered before a percentile is read
the p-th percentile is the smallest wait with at least p percent of the waits at or below it

origin.section: 10.5 A Load Test Is Judged by Its Slow Tail and Its Nulls

concepts: A load run is judged by percentiles over every request, with each null counted at the time it waited, and by the number of nulls; the mean and answered-only percentiles hide the timeouts.
